title: Modal Auxiliary Verbs: Can and Could for Ability
content:
## Modal Auxiliary Verbs: Can and Could for Ability

Learn how “can” expresses present ability or capacity and “could” expresses ability or capacity in the past, with examples and a fill-in-the-blank exercise.

### Understand the pattern

Can describes present ability or capacity. Could commonly describes general ability in the past. For success on one particular past occasion, was/were able to or managed to is often clearer than could; context can create exceptions.

### Worked answers and explanation

1. I could speak English well when I was young. The past-time phrase identifies an earlier general ability.
2. He is over eighty, but can still read without glasses. Can describes the ability he has now.

These answers address the two questions on this page, rather than the previous-quiz key printed on the poster.

### Try another

Complete: When I was six, I ___ already ride a bicycle. (can / could)

### Suggested answer

Could. The clause refers to a general past ability. For one specific success yesterday, 'I managed to repair the bicycle' would express the achievement more precisely.
